nameStory: Job's tears gets its poetic name from the hard, teardrop-shaped seed cases that look like pearly white teardrops. These glossy, bead-like structures have been used for centuries to make prayer beads and jewelry, connecting the plant's name to the biblical figure Job and his trials. The scientific name 'lacryma-jobi' literally means 'tears of Job' in Latin.
description: Job's tears is a tall, tropical grass that can grow several feet high with broad, corn-like leaves. This exotic member of the grass family is rarely seen in New England, appearing occasionally in gardens or as an escape from cultivation. The plant is most famous for its distinctive hard, oval seed cases that look like shiny white or grayish pearls hanging from the stems. Despite being a grass, it looks more like a small corn plant to most observers.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Hard, oval, bead-like seed cases that are pearly white to light gray, about the size of a large pea, with a glossy, smooth surface that feels like polished stone

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, lance-shaped leaves that clasp the stem, similar to corn leaves but typically narrower, with parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright grass growing 3-6 feet high with thick, jointed stems that feel sturdy and bamboo-like when squeezed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Inconspicuous grass flowers arranged in small clusters, with male and female flowers separate on the same plant, easily overlooked

habitat: Job's tears is extremely rare in New England, found only occasionally in protected garden settings or as a short-lived escape from cultivation. When present, it prefers warm, sheltered locations with rich, moist soil. This tropical plant cannot survive New England winters outdoors and is typically grown as an ornamental annual.

seasonality.spring: Seeds would be planted in late spring after all danger of frost has passed, with young plants emerging as small grass-like shoots.
seasonality.summer: Plant reaches full height with broad leaves fully developed, and inconspicuous flowers appear in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: The characteristic hard, bead-like seed cases develop and ripen, becoming the plant's most distinctive feature before frost kills the plant.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters - plant dies with first hard frost, leaving only the persistent hard seed cases.

funFact: The hard seed cases are so durable and naturally polished that they've been used as beads for over 4,000 years - archaeologists have found Job's tears jewelry in ancient Chinese tombs, making them possibly the world's oldest natural beads still in use today!
confusionNotes: The broad leaves might be confused with young corn plants, but Job's tears has the distinctive hard, bead-like seed cases that corn lacks. The seeds are unmistakable once formed - no other New England plant produces anything quite like these natural pearls.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Chinese pearl barley' in some markets, Job's tears is not related to true barley at all - they're just both grasses. The cultivated variety has soft, edible seeds used in Asian cooking, while the ornamental variety produces the hard, bead-like seeds prized for crafts.
compareHints: Job's tears is the only species in its genus found in New England gardens. Among grasses, it's most similar to corn in leaf shape and overall appearance, but corn grows much taller and produces familiar corn ears instead of the distinctive bead-like seed cases. Other ornamental grasses in New England lack both the broad corn-like leaves and the hard, pearl-like seeds.
